title: Boolean Conditions in C
learningObjectives: Explain the central rules behind boolean conditions in c in C.
Identify the relevant types, declarations, operators or library facilities.
Trace a worked example and explain its result.
Recognize common mistakes, portability concerns and unsafe assumptions.
Apply the concept in a small program and test normal and boundary cases.

understand.concept: C uses integer-like truth values in conditions: zero is false and nonzero is true. The standard _Bool type stores 0 or 1; stdbool.h provides the bool, true and false convenience names in C versions where it is available as a macro header. Relational and logical operators produce int results in C.
understand.whyItMatters: Reliable decisions depend on clear conditions. Explicit boolean intent makes code easier to read and helps avoid confusing numeric values, pointers and truth conditions.
understand.analogy: Think of a type as a contract that describes what kind of value an object can hold and which operations make sense for it.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is only an introduction; C types also determine representation, conversions, alignment and constraints.

explain.narrative:
C uses integer-like truth values in conditions: zero is false and nonzero is true. The standard _Bool type stores 0 or 1; stdbool.h provides the bool, true and false convenience names in C versions where it is available as a macro header. Relational and logical operators produce int results in C.

Reliable decisions depend on clear conditions. Explicit boolean intent makes code easier to read and helps avoid confusing numeric values, pointers and truth conditions.

When reviewing code, identify the declared types first, then trace conversions and the exact expression being evaluated. Compile with warnings enabled and test boundary values. Do not rely on assumptions about another compiler or machine.

examples.title: Core example
examples.explanation: The bool spelling is provided by stdbool.h in applicable C standards; the condition is true when the stored value is nonzero.

examples.title: A second case
examples.explanation: An integer condition is true when its value is nonzero. Comparing explicitly can improve clarity when the variable represents a count.

practise.guidedTask: Write conditions for a valid age range, a non-empty array length and a successful status flag. Test true, false and boundary cases.
practise.independentTask: Refactor a long nested condition into named boolean variables and explain how each part contributes to the final decision.
hints: Zero is false; nonzero is true in a C condition.
Logical operators produce int results in C.
Use parentheses to make compound conditions readable.
Test boundary values, not only typical values.
